note: Phase 10 (equivalence-gap plan) — a declared query's own `nulls :last` override, real for the first time (rust/src/kernel/query_ordering.rs's own NullsMode; before this, ANY declared `null_semantics` refused the whole query, unconditionally). `Banking::ATMCard.Active` is the real corpus declaration this exercises (examples/banking/bluebook/payment_cards.bluebook: `order_by :nickname; nulls :last`, `nickname` genuinely optional — that file's own comment: "Active's own query below relies on this to demonstrate nulls for real"). Three cards issued and activated for account acct-1: card-a (renamed to nickname "Zulu"), card-b (renamed to nickname "Alpha"), card-c (left unnamed — nickname stays nil). Ascending order_by :nickname with the DEFAULT null policy would sort nil FIRST (query_ordering.rs's own else-arm), giving [card-c(nil), card-b(Alpha), card-a(Zulu)] — the declared `nulls :last` override instead puts card-c LAST regardless of ascending direction: [card-b(Alpha), card-a(Zulu), card-c(nil)]. That reordering — nil moving from the front to the back of the SAME three rows — is the one thing this fixture actually proves; a generator that silently ignored `nulls :last` and fell back to the default policy would still return the right ROWS, just in the wrong order, which a Rust conformance run's own byte-for-byte comparison catches.
